author: Codex Designer rehearsal, 2026-11-09. All descriptions, proposed requirements and guesses are agent text.
stage_status: Stages 0 and 1 rehearsal only; no completion, sent ask, approval, waiver or ledger write.

root_draft.speaker: agent
root_draft.text: HugeThings makes huge plants and animals behave like the size you see: mass has consequences. A giant fungus has a solid stem and roots, open space beneath its cap, and a picture you can actually click; growing trunks respect the colony already around them. A huge animal has a body you can select, and a titan meets gaps, walls, roofs and trenches as a creature of its breadth: squeezing where it fits, breaking what it can, and being held by what really stops it. Its passage can wreck the colony simply because something that large walked through. A biome's own giants announce their approach with tremors. The largest dead titan becomes a landmark worked over days, with ordinary meat's rules for rot, while scavengers and visiting people compete for what remains. These are several connected promises, each owed its own demonstration. HugeThings supplies the common machinery; the biomes supply the living things, Large Pawns supplies their larger occupied bodies when loaded, and the plant and animal settings let the player tune their consequences.

F3: Real mass makes the colony painful: dense forest stalls, growth eats possessions or access, path decisions churn, or reload/settings leave ghosts or silently change behaviour. asks.title: What the paragraph has to get right
asks.picture: A colony lives among fungi whose trunks really take up ground. Later a titan crosses its outskirts, leaves damage, and eventually leaves remains worth going out to work.
asks.text: Which moment in that picture makes this HugeThings to you, and which sentence in the proposed root misstates what you expect?
asks.decision: Root emphasis and reject-level promise; approval still requires his real reply.
asks.why: F1/F2. 'Mass has consequences' could mean physical truth throughout play or mainly a dramatic titan story. The root must say the right thing without erasing either built half.
asks.guess: Physical truth is the foundation; titan damage and the harvest race are the story it produces. I would lead with that.
asks.tree_change: If physical truth leads, the root and first explanatory examples centre on visible size matching interaction. If the story leads, reorder the root around passage and aftermath while retaining plant, selection and other built coverage. A correction changes dependent claims; no answer means no approved root.
asks.author: Codex Designer rehearsal
asks.speaker: agent

asks.title: The first demonstration
asks.picture: Three labelled scene drafts: A, a working forest colony with solid trunks, open caps, clicks and growth; B, your destructive crossing followed by a force-kill and the rush to the remains; C, your older carcass already occupied by locals. These are descriptions, not staged or accepted scenes.
asks.text: Which scene would you put first when deciding whether HugeThings has understood you, and what single failure there would make you stop the demonstration?
asks.decision: Owner flagship pick and its first rejection case, not whether to include the other capabilities/scenarios.
asks.why: F1/F2. Your two titan scenes are already valid; their order and the mod's flagship have not been picked in the evidence I found.
asks.guess: B: the crossing makes the death and gathering crowds an understandable consequence. I recommend it first, with the forest as a separate demonstration.
asks.tree_change: The chosen scene becomes showcase 1 only after his recorded pick. The others remain candidates or ordinary scenes, with separate feature acceptance and an interaction scene. Root approval alone will not be stored as a flagship pick.
asks.author: Codex Designer rehearsal
asks.speaker: agent

asks.title: A root that must leave a doorway open
asks.picture: A fungus grows beside a workshop. Its picture now puts a root across the doorway, but the safety rules leave that cell open rather than seal the workshop. Nothing is destroyed and nobody is moved.
asks.text: When you notice a colonist walking through that drawn root, what explanation or visible clue would make this exception make sense to you?
asks.decision: Player-facing treatment of a refused trunk cell; existing safety and open-canopy rules stay.
asks.why: F1/F3. 'Solid where it touches ground' meets the already-built protection of doors and access. The mechanism is readable from code; the acceptable player explanation is not settled there.
asks.guess: Safety wins, but clicking the fungus should explain that its trunk cannot fill the doorway. I would start with that small explanation rather than another warning letter.
asks.tree_change: If the explanation is essential, add an inspect/readability requirement tied to an actually refused cell and an obstruction/free-space control. If the exception needs no explanation, add no cue requirement and state the bounded solidity promise clearly. If the art itself must change, return to a labelled exploration before binding a visual leaf.
asks.author: Codex Designer rehearsal
asks.speaker: agent

asks.title: What the warning lets you do
asks.picture: You get tremors from the east while colonists are working outside. The titan has not arrived. The current warning lasts six in-game hours; that number is a provisional setting.
asks.text: When it appears, which preparations should be finished, and which dangers should still surprise you?
asks.decision: Warning's actionable information and usable time, rather than re-asking whether warnings exist.
asks.why: F2. A delay and screen shake can satisfy 'warning' while giving the player no useful choice. Direction, identity, route certainty and available preparation time change that promise.
asks.guess: Recall exposed workers and livestock and decide whether to get out of its way; no promise that a thin wall protects the base. I would preserve uncertainty about its exact route.
asks.tree_change: A recall window gives a scene with dispersed workers and a measured chance to shelter. A construction window requires a longer preparation case. Exact route knowledge would require honest route information and rewarning when it changes. His answer sets the experience bar, not an invented fixed number today.
asks.author: Codex Designer rehearsal
asks.speaker: agent

asks.title: The moment competitors become enemies
asks.picture: People have arrived to feed from the remains. Your colonists build a fence that denies them access. Nobody has attacked anybody. In the current build they are ordinary non-hostile visitors; there is no carcass-specific dispute rule.
asks.text: What should those people do first, and what act by the colony would make a fight over the carcass deserved?
asks.decision: Denial trigger, response and fair warning for carcass-specific conflict.
asks.why: F2. 'The locals aren't too happy' does not yet say whether a fence means protest, trespass, negotiation or violence. The event's agent summary cannot decide that as your words.
asks.guess: They object, then try to reach the food; the colony gets a readable chance to relent before deliberate exclusion becomes conflict. I would not make a first fence an instant silent war.
asks.tree_change: Protest/ultimatum needs a visible dispute state and a control where access is restored. Forced access needs behaviour around the fence. Negotiation needs a defined bargain. Violence needs an exact trigger, scope and stop condition. If ordinary visitor behaviour is enough, no new custom-hostility leaf is inferred.
asks.author: Codex Designer rehearsal
asks.speaker: agent

asks.title: What a prior claim means
asks.picture: Your arriving clan finds the older carcass you described, with people already working beside it. A colonist walks up to work at the opposite side without attacking anyone.
asks.text: What do the people already there regard as theirs, and what could your clan do to earn a share?
asks.decision: Prior claim and peaceful access in the older-carcass scene, distinct from q05's response to active exclusion.
asks.why: F2. Prior presence can mean territorial ownership, a claimed portion, or simply rivals who resent sharing. Each gives the newcomer a different first decision.
asks.guess: A prior group has a recognisable claim the newcomer must respect, buy into or challenge. I would make the claim visible before the first harvest order can offend them.
asks.tree_change: A whole-site claim needs ownership and permission; a portion needs separate accounted shares; open competition needs no title system, only rivalry. A bargain adds only the specific exchange he describes. The old carcass remains a hand-staged exploration/acceptance fixture until separate authority exists for spawning it in play.
asks.author: Codex Designer rehearsal
asks.speaker: agent

asks.title: A carcass worth rearranging the day for
asks.picture: A large corpse lies outside a forty-colonist settlement. The current site permits one worker at a time, with a default hour of Mining work for a small batch. Rot must obey your ordinary-meat ruling; we cannot create urgency by making it rot faster.
asks.text: You decide to make a serious effort to recover it: what does that day's work look like, and what is left when the colony goes home?
asks.decision: Harvest labour, throughput and visitor competition at colony scale.
asks.why: F2/F3. 'Worked over days' can hide an idle queue behind one worker; an army harvesting instantly can erase the race. The intended commitment is not specified by the current batch sizes.
asks.guess: A meaningful expedition with several useful jobs, enough recovery to reward choosing it, and plenty left for tomorrow and the competitors. I would test both a modest colony and a strong mobilisation.
asks.tree_change: Parallel work requires reservations/concurrency and pool-conservation acceptance. One specialist with supporting hauling instead needs useful throughput and support jobs demonstrated. The amount recovered and arrival pressure are tuned from his picture, with ordinary-temperature and frozen controls; no new artificial spoilage clock.
asks.author: Codex Designer rehearsal
asks.speaker: agent

asks.title: You change the way in after the tremors
asks.picture: You hear tremors from the east, then finish a barrier across the warned entry. The current event checks the route again and may find a different entry or let the tremors fade. The new entry can be on another side of the colony.
asks.text: What should happen in the story when that approach becomes blocked, and what must the colony be told before danger comes from somewhere else?
asks.decision: Warning honesty and arrival timing after route invalidation.
asks.why: F1/F2. An east warning followed by a west arrival can make preparation pointless; making every barrier cancel a titan can make mass meaningless. Built revalidation has not settled the desired play.
asks.guess: It obeys its existing wall/rock rules, and a changed approach gives me a fresh honest warning. I would not silently swap edges at arrival time.
asks.tree_change: Same-edge persistence needs a real blocked-route clearing test. Another edge needs changed-direction communication and a defined preparation window. A justified retreat needs a reason the player can read. Thick rock and curated protections stay intact under every answer.
asks.author: Codex Designer rehearsal
asks.speaker: agent

neighbours.text: Occupied squares, projected ladder; optional external dependency. Vanilla one-cell fallback retained.
Cliff masks, floor/deck views, pocket reachability and fall/step handling consume stride. Shared pawnless terrain path cost can still favour short detours; relative-rule branch only.
Actual opted-in plants and art-derived contact data, not built-in HugeThings species.
Existing common draw arithmetic and settings renderer compiled by explicit project links; do not duplicate.
Crown data consumer owns actual shade/heat. HugeThings measures tree crowns only.
VisitColony and ExitMapNear already supply generic visitors/migration; current custom carcass claim/dispute behaviour is absent. No second generic visitor system proposed.
